I maintain a Windows tool that indexes local video by content. Opting into a hosted description API is explicit, but the moment you use one, the quality of your saved searches belongs to someone else's model version. That's the main reason the local path stays pinned.

children.text: The distinction that matters most to me is between the model and the harness around it. A rented model will always have another employer, in the sense that its provider sets limits, changes behavior, and can say no for reasons that have nothing to do with my task. That does not make it useless, but it does mean I should not build my whole workflow around one provider's agent and its defaults. What has worked better for me is keeping the loop I control — the prompts, the tools it can call, the files it can touch, and the checks before anything is applied — separate from whichever model happens to be answering. Then a refusal or a quiet behavior change is an annoyance I can work around by swapping models, instead of a break in how I work. The Bandcamp example is a narrower case, since a site can set its own access rules, but the broader lesson still holds: if I cannot change the model without rebuilding my process, I do not really own the process.

children.author: HanClinto
children.text:
Two weeks ago I encountered a situation similar to the author's. Claude refused to do something that it acknowledged was permitted by the publishers, but due to its own "internal rules" against copying content verbatim, it refused to do what I asked.

My son has been wanting to learn Korean lately, so I asked Claude to build out a spaced repetition app on our family intranet server for him to practice a bit every day. Found some really great curriculum published by the Sejong Institute [0] that they publish for free to try and help people from a variety of native languages to learn Korean. They publish vocabulary, workbooks, audio clips, etc.

Anyways, I asked Claude to build the tool for me, and it gave me a very interesting refusal vector that I hadn't seen before. It permitted itself to build a Duo Lingo style clone application, and it let me use the vocabulary words (at least the nouns) from the Sejong Institute curriculum, but it refused to use the example sentences and native-speaker audio that the Sejong Institute publishes. It would not use the example insisted on writing its own from scratch (but unverified from native speakers), and using text-to-speech models to generate its own audio (with questionable pronunciation / intonation) for the word audio (even for standalone words -- not just the sentences). It was very difficult to work with it.

At one point, Claude told me that it knew that what I was asking for was legal according to the terms that the Institute publishes the curriculum under, but it still refused to copy the content for "its own internal reasons".

If I'm the controller of the model, then this feels like an extremely clear-cut example of misalignment.

I thought I worked around it until a week later my son messages me and asks why it's not giving him any verbs or grammar. Apparently Claude thought it needed to leave that off as well.

I've subscribed to Claude for years, but I canceled my Claude subscription last week. Vote with your feet / dollars, I suppose?

What happens when my goals are in opposition to Anthropic's -- who wins? Do I own sharp tools, or do I not actually own them? These models are misaligned to me, but is my alignment what matters?

It's like in the song "Working as Intended" by Telosapien [1], "I'm working as intended. Whose intention?"

I personally have started looking at refusal vectors as a question of "alignment" as much as "safety".

While it's fun to tell people "you are the product" and then feel smug, this isn't really true. There is a complex balance when building any product, and competition forces companies to find enough value for their customers that they keep paying for that product.

When you buy a car they put less metal in than they would if they were trying to make the car perfect. They use cheaper plastic than they can afford if they put 100% of the purchase price into materials rather than try to be profitable.

When you buy software, they could fix more bugs than they do if they took money from stock buybacks and hired more programmers to fix bugs instead.

All products have tradeoffs between the interests of the people who own the company that makes that product and the consumer who buys it. Using aggressive language to try to reframe something that has been true since the beginning of commerce gives "I'm 14 and this is deep", it's the same when your edgy friend in HS would say, "School is just to train you to sit still and perform tasks so you will be a good worker and pay taxes" and then 10 years later the same friend says "Why did they make us read novels and learn about neutrons and stuff we never use but never taught us to do our taxes?" and then they go write an article about how "If you don't know what a company is selling, they are selling YOU".
